title: Canonical Microcircuit
intro: Douglas and Martin's canonical microcircuit is the classic answer to 'what does the local cortical circuit do?': a handful of recurrently connected excitatory and inhibitory populations that amplify weak thalamic input, select among competing inputs and pass the result through the layers. It is the template most spiking column models, including Potjans–Diesmann, are built on.

blocks.text: Picture a column as a small amplifier rather than a relay station. Thalamic input arrives, but it is weak: only a small fraction of the excitatory synapses even on layer 4 cells come from the thalamus. The rest of the excitation a cortical neuron receives comes from other cortical neurons, most of them nearby. Douglas and Martin's insight was that this local recurrent excitation is not noise or redundancy — it is the machinery that takes a faint, specific input, amplifies it, sharpens it against competing inputs with the help of inhibition, and hands the result on to other layers and other areas.

They called this the canonical microcircuit: a deliberately simplified wiring diagram, the same in every area of neocortex (that is the 'canonical' part, echoing Mountcastle's hypothesis — see "Mountcastle's Hypothesis" in section 1), that captures what the local circuit does with its input. It is not a detailed connectome. It is a functional summary — three or four populations and the arrows between them — which is exactly why it is so useful to modellers.
Where it came from: cat V1 intracellular recordings

Douglas, Martin and Whitteridge (1989) recorded intracellularly from neurons in cat primary visual cortex in vivo while electrically stimulating the thalamic afferents (the optic radiation). Neurons in all layers responded with a similar sequence: a brief excitation followed by a long-lasting inhibition, of the order of 100–200 ms. A purely feedforward circuit, in which thalamus excites layer 4 and layer 4 excites everything else in a chain, could not reproduce how similar the responses were across layers or their time course. A small model with recurrently connected populations could.

The model had three populations: superficial pyramidal cells (layers 2/3, plus the layer 4 spiny cells), deep pyramidal cells (layers 5/6), and a pool of GABAergic inhibitory cells. All three receive thalamic input; all are recurrently connected to one another; the inhibitory pool has both fast (GABA-A-like) and slow (GABA-B-like) components. Douglas and Martin (1991) developed this into a functional microcircuit for cat visual cortex, and Douglas, Koch, Mahowald, Martin and Suarez (1995) made the central computational claim explicit: recurrent cortical excitation amplifies the weak thalamic signal, and inhibition keeps this amplification stable and selective.

The canonical circuit is often summarised as a dominant feedforward path through the layers, with recurrence at every stage. A common simplified reading (Douglas & Martin 2004; Harris & Shepherd 2015, who also stress its many exceptions) is:

items: Thalamus → L4 (and, more weakly, directly to L5/L6 and L2/3): the sensory 'driver' input enters, mainly in layer 4 in primary sensory areas.
L4 → L2/3: layer 4 spiny stellate and pyramidal cells project upward to superficial pyramidal cells.
L2/3 → L2/3 (strong recurrence) and L2/3 → other cortical areas: superficial pyramids talk to each other heavily and send the main feedforward cortico-cortical output.
L2/3 → L5: superficial cells project down to layer 5, whose thick-tufted pyramids send output to subcortical targets (and to higher-order thalamus).
L5 → L6 and L6 → thalamus / L4: layer 6 corticothalamic cells close a loop back to the thalamus and also feed layer 4, gating its own input.
Inhibitory interneurons in every layer, receiving local excitation and inhibiting nearby cells: they set gain, enforce competition and shape timing.

blocks.text: Treat this as a skeleton, not a law. Thalamic axons also contact layers 5 and 6 directly, layer 5 can be driven without layer 2/3, and the balance of pathways differs between areas and species. The canonical circuit is a hypothesis about shared function, not a claim that all areas are wired identically.
Binzegger et al. 2004: putting numbers on the circuit

Binzegger, Douglas and Martin (2004) turned the qualitative diagram into a quantitative map for cat area 17. They used three-dimensional reconstructions of individual, physiologically characterised neurons and estimated how many synapses each cell type makes onto each other cell type in each layer, assuming that synapses form roughly in proportion to how much an axon overlaps a target's dendrites (a version of Peters' rule). Their main conclusions:

items: Most excitatory synapses in every layer come from cortical neurons, and a large share come from neurons in the same layer: recurrent excitation dominates.
Thalamic afferents provide only a small fraction of the synapses, even in layer 4 (single-digit percentages are the usual estimate; treat the exact value as uncertain).
Superficial (L2/3) pyramidal cells form the largest population and the largest source of synapses; their self-connections are the single strongest pathway.
The diagram is dominated by a few strong loops, which supports the idea of a small canonical circuit with heavy recurrence.

blocks.text: This synapse-count table later became one of the main inputs to the Potjans–Diesmann connection probabilities (see "Potjans–Diesmann Microcircuit" in this section). Because it relies on Peters'-rule-style estimates, it predicts potential contacts, not measured functional connections; paired recordings (for example Thomson et al. 2002; Lefort et al. 2009 in mouse barrel cortex) supply the complementary physiological side.

The essential computation fits in a one-population rate model. Let r be the firing rate of a pool of excitatory cells with recurrent weight w (the total recurrent gain) and external (thalamic) drive h:

blocks.source:
τ dr/dt = −r + [ w·r + h ]₊

steady state (w < 1):   r* = h / (1 − w)
amplification factor:   G = 1 / (1 − w)

w = 0.0  →  G = 1   (feedforward relay)
w = 0.8  →  G = 5
w = 0.9  →  G = 10
w ≥ 1    →  runaway (needs inhibition or saturation)

with an inhibitory pool I driven by E:
τE dE/dt = −E + [ wEE·E − wEI·I + h ]₊
τI dI/dt = −I + [ wIE·E ]₊

blocks.text: Two consequences matter for builders. First, recurrent gain buys sensitivity: a weak input produces a large response, which is how a few percent of thalamic synapses can drive cortex. Second, gain near 1 makes the network slow and fragile: the effective time constant becomes τ/(1 − w), so with τ = 10 ms and w = 0.9 the pool integrates over about 100 ms, and small parameter changes push it into runaway. Inhibition is what allows a high excitatory gain to stay stable. With several excitatory pools competing through shared inhibition, the same circuit becomes a soft winner-take-all: the most strongly driven pool is amplified and the others are suppressed (Douglas & Martin 2004; this is the link to "Inhibition and k-WTA" in section 3).
Using it when you build a column

items: Start from the canonical skeleton: one excitatory and one inhibitory population per layer (or per layer group: L4, L2/3, L5, L6), with thalamic input mainly to L4 and recurrent E→E, E→I, I→E and I→I connections within each layer. This is precisely the structure Potjans and Diesmann later filled in with numbers.

Make thalamic input a minority of the excitatory drive (for example 5–15% of excitatory synapses onto L4 cells) and let recurrence do the amplification. If your column only responds when thalamic weights dominate, it is a feedforward relay, not a canonical circuit.

Measure the effective recurrent gain: silence the recurrent weights and compare the response to the same input. Gains of a few-fold are plausible; gains above about 10 usually mean you are near instability.

Use inhibition for stability and selectivity together. A soft-WTA built this way behaves like the k-winners-take-all used in HTM (see "Inhibition and k-WTA" in section 3), but emerges from dynamics rather than being imposed by sorting.
Keep the excitatory and inhibitory time constants distinct (inhibition at least as fast as excitation); slow inhibition with strong recurrent excitation produces oscillations or bursts.
Record the response to a brief input pulse: the Douglas–Martin signature is a short excitation followed by a long inhibition in every layer. It is a cheap sanity check of your E/I loop.

The canonical circuit is a functional abstraction. It says how the column amplifies and selects, not what it represents or learns. It is compatible with HTM, predictive coding and many other theories, which is both its strength and its limitation.
Its data come mostly from cat V1. Mouse, rat barrel and primate cortex differ in layer 4 prominence, interneuron composition and long-range wiring (Harris & Shepherd 2015).
Peters'-rule estimates overcount some pathways and miss specificity: connectomic reconstructions show that axons often choose targets more selectively than overlap alone predicts.
Strong recurrent excitation in spiking networks is notoriously easy to make unstable. Expect to tune inhibition first (see "Common Pitfalls" in section 7).
